stem: To control the media in India, ‘Acts’ were passed in –
expl: To control newspapers that exposed the government’s repressive policies, the Press Act of 1835 (Act No. XI of 1835) was promulgated. After this, the Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867 was passed. Viceroy Lord Lytton passed the Vernacular Press Act in 1878, under which no newspaper could be published without the government’s permission if it contained criticism of the British government. In addition, an Act to control the press was passed by Lord Minto in 1908, under which the government had the power to confiscate any publication that was accused of inciting public feeling against the government.

stem: Who among the following repealed the Vernacular Press Act of 1878?
expl: Lord Ripon repealed the Vernacular Press Act in 1882 and gave Indian-language newspapers the same freedom as English-language newspapers. It is noteworthy that the Vernacular Press Act was passed in 1878 during Lord Lytton’s tenure (1876–1880). This Act was called the “Gagging Act.” Its most objectionable feature was that it discriminated between newspapers in Indian languages and those in English, and it did not give the offender the right to appeal. Under this Act, a district magistrate, or the Police Commissioner of a presidency town—within whose local jurisdiction a newspaper was printed and published—had the power to make any Indian-language newspaper sign a bond (Bond) stating that it would not publish any anti-government material. The security deposit of printing presses that opposed the law could be cancelled. Under this Act, cases were registered against Som Prakash, Bharat Mihir, Dhaka Prakash, Sahchar, and many other newspapers.

stem:
Which of the following statements about the Vernacular Press Act is/are correct?
1. It was enacted by Lord Lytton.
2. It came to be known as a ‘Gagging Act’.
3. The Act was repealed by Lord Ripon.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
expl: Lord Lytton enacted the Vernacular Press Act, 1878, which empowered the government to seize newspapers publishing so-called “anti-government material”. It may be noted that English-language newspapers were exempted from this Act and were not regulated under its provisions. Under the Vernacular Press Act, any magistrate or police commissioner had the authority to order any printer or publisher of a newspaper not to print a specified kind of material and could seize any printed matter considered objectionable. This Act was nicknamed the “Gagging Act”. Its most objectionable features were—(i) discrimination between the English and vernacular press, and (ii) no right of appeal. Under the VPA, action was initiated against newspapers such as Som Prakash, Bharat Mihir, Dhaka Prakash, and others. This law was repealed in 1882 by Lord Ripon (Viceroy, 1880–84), Lord Lytton’s successor.

stem: Who founded the Asiatic Society of Bengal?

options.label: d
options.text: More than one of the above

expl: The Asiatic Society of Bengal was founded in 1784 on the initiative of Sir William Jones. The Society’s name underwent several changes over time, such as The Asiatic Society of Bengal (1832–1935), The Royal Asiatic Society of Bengal (1936–1951), and since July 1951 it has been known as the Asiatic Society. Since 1984, the Asiatic Society has been accorded the status of an institution of national importance under an Act of the Indian Parliament.
